title: Kingdom of Naples
capsule: The Kingdom of Naples emerged in 1282 when the Sicilian Vespers expelled the Angevin dynasty from Sicily, confining Charles I of Anjou to the southern Italian mainland; by 1285 a distinct Neapolitan kingdom was consolidated under French Angevin rule, covering modern Campania, Basilicata, Calabria, Puglia, and Abruzzo. The kingdom endured prolonged dynastic conflict between the Angevin and Aragonese lines: Alfonso V of Aragon conquered Naples in 1442, uniting it briefly with Sicily, and his illegitimate son Ferdinand I (Ferrante) inherited Naples in 1458, navigating the Papal and Venetian threats. Ferdinand's death in 1494 triggered Charles VIII of France's invasion, opening the Italian Wars; France and Aragon partitioned Naples in 1501, but Ferdinand II of Aragon defeated the French at the Battle of the Garigliano (1503) and absorbed Naples into the Crown of Aragon by 1504.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Kingdom of Naples' boundaries are well-attested in papal investiture documents and Angevin-Aragonese chancery records; its southern Italian extent is clearly defined, though jurisdictional overlaps with the Papacy in certain border territories were contested.
